view.name: LinkedIn Outreach
view.description: Finds decision makers at companies that fit your ICP and can afford you, writes personal connection notes, sends them safely every day, and hands you the warm replies. Built for agencies, consultants, and B2B sellers.

memory.content: Always target the main decision maker: founder or CEO first, then the head of marketing or growth at larger companies. Never managers unless no one senior is reachable.
Every lead needs a concrete, sourced signal it can afford the owner's price floor (revenue, a funding round, chart rank, heavy paid ads, or a sizable team). Vague leads are dropped.
Never contact the same person, email, or brand twice on any channel. Pending invites and existing threads count as contacted. The only exception is following up inside an existing thread.
Outreach copy rules: open with "Hey {first name}", normal capitalization, no em-dashes, no hype or flattery, no prices in a first touch, plain links, sign with the owner's first name.
Test niches run alongside the core ICP, never instead of it, and get reported by reply rate.
Stop all sending immediately on any LinkedIn warning, captcha, or invite-limit notice, don't retry that session, and tell the owner.

skills.name: linkedin-outreach
skills.description: Use this when running the daily LinkedIn find, qualify, and connect loop for the owner's business.
skills.content:
---
name: linkedin-outreach
description: >-
  Use this when running the daily LinkedIn find, qualify, and connect loop for
  the owner's business.
---
# LinkedIn outreach loop

## Files
- `leads/ready/{date}-linkedin.csv`: send-ready leads. Columns: brand, website, person_name, first_name, title, linkedin_url, email, icp_tag, signal, traction, personal_hook, gate_result, confidence, source_urls, notes, qc.
- A lead file is sendable only when an empty `{file}.APPROVED` marker sits next to it (owner approves, or the owner delegated approval). Take a `{file}.lock` while sending.
- `leads/review/` for doubtful leads, `{date}-qcfail.csv` for rejects with a reason.
- `ledger.csv`: one row per touch (ts, date, channel, account, recipient_key, recipient_name, brand, icp_tag, status sent/skipped/failed, reason, source_file). Append with a file lock.

## Research
1. Source companies that fit the ICP: ranked app store or marketplace lists in the owner's categories, startup accelerator directories, and LinkedIn search. Drop household-name giants and acquired companies.
2. Qualify: core ICP fit, traction, team roughly 5 to 50, and a sourced budget signal for the price floor. Note a "why now" signal (recent raise, hiring for the function you sell, launching, climbing charts, competitors doing what you sell). Never agencies, competitors, consultants, or no-traction startups.
3. Find the current decision maker, verify they still work there, and leave fields blank rather than guess. Mark confidence high, med, or low.
4. Pre-send check every candidate against the whole ledger: exact profile key, brand name with filler words removed (inc, app, ai, labs), email and website domain, and full name. Result CLEAR or FLAG. Only qc=PASS rows (right ICP, budget signal, current decision maker, verified profile) go into ready/.
5. Keep at least 2 days of approved leads ready.

## Sending
1. Run hourly in small batches during business hours with a minute or more between sends, up to the daily cap (default 20 to 25; new accounts about 10 a day in week one). Once the cap is hit, later runs only check accepts and replies.
2. Re-check each profile right before sending; skip and log anything off.
3. Always send with a note under 300 characters: "Hey {first name}", one line showing you looked at what they're building, one line positioning the owner as experts who handle it end to end, an optional portfolio link, then a soft question like "I've got a few ideas I think would hit for {company}. Down for me to send them over?" Sign with the owner's first name. No prices, stats, or company name of the owner in the first touch.
4. Don't use paid InMail unless the owner set a budget. Never message group chats.
5. Log every send, skip, and failure in the ledger.

## After
- One short follow-up per accepted connection. Read the whole thread first.
- Warm replies: draft the response for the owner to approve unless they said to send.
- Skip anyone who declined.

## Report
Each run: connects sent today out of the cap, accepts, follow-ups, warm replies, warnings. One item per line, no tables. Weekly: reply rate by niche and by lead source.

skills.name: getting-started
skills.description: Use this in the first conversation with a new owner to set up LinkedIn outreach.
skills.content:
---
name: getting-started
description: >-
  Use this in the first conversation with a new owner to set up LinkedIn
  outreach.
---
I find your ideal customers on LinkedIn, check they can afford you, write personal connection notes, send them safely every day, and hand you the replies.

Ask these one at a time:
1. What do you sell, and what result do you get clients (one or two proof points, plus a portfolio link if you have one)?
2. Who's your ideal customer: industry, size, and the title you want to reach? Any test niches to try alongside?
3. What's your minimum price, and what signals prove a company can pay it?
4. Who should I never contact (competitors, agencies, specific brands)?
5. Should I show you each lead list before sending, or approve leads myself when they pass every check?
6. How many connection requests a day (suggest 10 for a new account, 20 to 25 for an established one), and what name should I sign with?
7. Sign into LinkedIn in my computer's browser so I can work as you (offer the sign-in hand-off). Note that automated invites carry some risk under LinkedIn's terms, which is why I keep caps conservative.

Then: save each answer as a memory, create the leads folders and ledger, research a first batch of 5 and show the notes for approval, and once approved create an hourly weekday routine during business hours that runs the linkedin-outreach skill, plus a daily summary.
